description: Bibi-Khanym, identified with Saray Mulk Khanum, Timur's chief wife, is the tragic royal lady behind Samarkand's great Friday mosque. Legend holds that she commissioned the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in 1399 as a surprise, then promised the architect a kiss that left a telltale mark; Timur's return doomed the enamored builder, and she died of grief. Her name crowns Central Asia's grandest monument.

research_notes: Attested figure tied to the real Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand (commissioned 1399). Saray Mulk Khanum was a Chingizid princess and Timur's chief consort; the architect's-kiss foundation legend appears in multiple travel and folklore accounts with variations. Corrects input's vague 'folk-hero' archetype to the documented foundation legend.

description: Bay-Terek, the 'rich poplar,' is the world tree of Altai and wider Turkic tradition, the axis mundi linking heaven, earth, and the underworld. It stands at the center of creation; its roots anchor the deep, its trunk is the shaman's route, and in its branches a double-headed eagle guards a golden egg while the serpent Erlik coils below to steal it. Kazakhs know the same tree as Baiterek.

research_notes: Attested Turkic axis-mundi figure; appears in the Altai epic Maadai-Kara and in Turkic cosmological lore (eagle at crown, snake/Erlik at root, nine branches and roots). Stern and possessive, he raised his daughter Angara until she fled him for the hero Yenisei; enraged, he hurled the Shaman Stone after her, yet she escaped to the sea. The lake remains a sacred, living entity honored with offerings.
